(c) Does the brace satisfy the design rule? (d) Hari's readings are off by up to 3 degrees. Should he pay for re-welding? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Vertically opposite angles should be equal: AOC with BOD (64 and 66, differ) and AOD with BOC (116 and 113, differ). Linear pairs should add to 180: AOC + AOD = 180 is fine, but AOC + BOC = 177 and BOD + AOD = 182 are not. (b) 64, 116, 64, 116 degrees. (c) Yes, the smallest angle is 64, which is at least 60. (d) No. Even if his reading were 3 degrees too high, the smallest angle would be at least 61 degrees, still at least 60, and the book says such small differences come from measuring, so ₹1,200 need not be spent.

Part (b): gives 64, 116, 64, 116 degrees
Part (c): checks the smallest angle 64 against 60
Part (d): says do not re-weld since 64 - 3 = 61 is still at least 60

Part (b): names the faulty readings with the vertically opposite or linear pair reason
Part (c): picks the north-east and south-west corners

questions.a: (a) The set square fits angle POR exactly, so it is 90 degrees and the lines are perpendicular; angle ROQ forms a linear pair with it, so it is 90 degrees. Part (b): gets k = 20 from 3k + 30 = 90

questions.q: Rohan wants to show that sides PS and QR of a rectangle PQRS are parallel. questions.a: Rohan's angles SPQ and RQP lie between the lines PS and QR on the same side of PQ; they are interior angles on the same side, not corresponding angles, and the book proves parallel lines only from equal corresponding angles. The angle that corresponds to angle SPQ is angle RQT at Q, above PQ and on the right. Angle RQT forms a linear pair with angle RQP, so it is 180 - 90 = 90 degrees. Corresponding angles SPQ and RQT are equal (90 and 90), so PS is parallel to QR. In the same way, extending PS beyond S and using PS as the transversal, the corresponding angles at P and at S are equal, so PQ is parallel to SR.

Identifies angle RQT as the corresponding angle of SPQ

So at least one reading is inexact, and the data do not show which; he should re-measure both rungs (and maybe a third) and trust the rails as parallel only if all rungs agree.

questions.a: (a) 180 degrees, because they are interior angles on the same side of a transversal across parallel lines. (b) 180 / 12 = 15, so 105 degrees and 75 degrees. (c) For 3 : 2 each part is 180 / 5 = 36, so the larger angle is 108 degrees; for 11 : 9 each part is 180 / 20 = 9, so the larger angle is 99 degrees. (d) The 11 : 9 design, because it is the only one whose larger angle (99 degrees) is not more than 100; the other two have 105 and 108 degrees.
s: Part (a): says 180 degrees with the reason
Part (b): gets 105 and 75 degrees
Part (c): gets 108 degrees and 99 degrees
Part (d): picks 11 : 9 because only it meets the 100 degree limit

questions.q: A square sheet is folded in half horizontally once. Counting its top edge, its bottom edge and the crease, how many parallel lines does it show?
In the paper-folding activity, how many parallel horizontal lines are there after 3 horizontal folds, counting the two edges?
Which rule gives the number of parallel horizontal lines after n horizontal folds, counting the two edges?

questions.a: It is perpendicular to the vertical side

Two lines in a picture look as if they lean towards each other. A straight edge across them gives corresponding angles of 72 degrees and 72 degrees. What is the correct conclusion?
questions.a: The lines are parallel in spite of how they look
o: The lines are parallel in spite of how they look

Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: Using the pattern 2^n + 1, a sheet with 4 horizontal folds shows 17 parallel lines.
Statement 2: Lines that look slanted in a picture can never be parallel.
Statement 3: Corresponding angles made by a transversal can be used to test whether lines that do not look parallel are parallel.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.a: A is true but R is false.

questions.q: (a) How many parallel horizontal lines are there after 2 horizontal folds, edges included? (b) How many are there after 5 folds?
questions.a: (a) 2^2 + 1 = 5 parallel lines. (b) 2^5 + 1 = 33 parallel lines.
s: Part (a): gets 5 lines
Part (b): gets 33 lines

questions.q: A square sheet has been folded horizontally twice and opened. (a) How is a horizontal crease related to the top edge? (b) A vertical fold is now made. How is it related to the horizontal creases?
questions.a: (a) A horizontal crease is parallel to the top edge. (b) The vertical fold is perpendicular to the horizontal creases.
s: Part (a): says parallel
Part (b): says perpendicular

questions.q: (a) Why can we not always decide just by looking whether two lines in a picture are parallel? (b) What does the chapter suggest we use to decide?
questions.a: (a) Some lines look parallel when they are not, and some that look slanted are parallel, so it is difficult to be sure by eye. (b) We use a transversal and compare the corresponding angles.
s: Part (a): says looks can mislead
Part (b): names a transversal and corresponding angles

questions.q: In a border pattern, two lines p and q seem to lean towards each other. A straight line t cuts them, and the lower-left angles it makes with p and with q are both 80 degrees. (a) What do you conclude about p and q? (b) What did your eyes suggest, and which should you trust?
questions.a: (a) The lower-left angles are corresponding angles and they are equal (80 and 80), so p and q are parallel. (b) The eyes suggested that the lines lean towards each other and would meet; the angle test should be trusted, because looks can mislead.
s: Part (a): concludes parallel from equal corresponding angles
Part (b): says the eye test misleads and the angle test is trusted

questions.q: A teacher wants a square sheet that shows exactly 65 parallel horizontal lines, edges included, after some horizontal folds. (a) Find the number of folds n. (b) Show how you checked your answer.
s: Part (a): gets n = 6
Part (b): checks 2^6 + 1 = 65

questions.q: A student counted the parallel lines after the first, second and third folds as 3, 5 and 7, and from this decided that every fold adds just 2 more lines. Is this pattern correct? Say what the true counts are and how they grow.
questions.a: No. The true counts are 3, 5, 9, 17. The first two fit his idea, but after the third fold there are 9, not 7. The number added doubles each time: 2, 4, 8, and the count follows 2^n + 1.
s: Says the pattern is wrong
Gives the true counts 3, 5, 9, 17
Says the increase doubles each time, as in 2^n + 1

questions.q: Show that a square sheet folded horizontally some number of times cannot show exactly 20 parallel lines, edges included.
questions.a: The count after n folds is 2^n + 1. For 20 lines we would need 2^n = 19. But 16 = 2^4 and 32 = 2^5, so 19 is not a power of 2 and no number of folds gives 20.
s: Writes 2^n + 1 = 20, so 2^n = 19
Notes the powers of 2 around 19 are 16 and 32
Concludes 20 is impossible

questions.q: A square sheet is folded horizontally 3 times and opened. Find (a) the total number of parallel horizontal lines including the two edges, (b) the number of creases alone, (c) the number of strips between neighbouring lines.
questions.a: (a) 2^3 + 1 = 9 lines. (b) Creases alone are 9 - 2 = 7. (c) 9 lines make 8 strips between neighbouring lines.
s: Part (a): gets 9 lines
Part (b): gets 7 creases
Part (c): gets 8 strips

questions.q: Tara folds a square sheet horizontally in half again and again, opening it each time and counting the parallel lines, the two edges included. She gets 3, 5, 9 and 17 after 1, 2, 3 and 4 folds. She predicts that the count after 5 folds will be 25 because 'the increase was 8 the last time, so I add 8 again'. Find her error and give the correct count after 5 folds. State the rule for n folds, use it for 6 folds, and say how many creases alone (the edges left out) the sheet shows after 4 folds.
questions.a: Her error: the increases are 2, 4, 8, which double each time, so the next increase is 16, not 8; the count after 5 folds is 17 + 16 = 33. The rule is 2^n + 1. For 6 folds it gives 2^6 + 1 = 65. After 4 folds there are 17 lines, of which 2 are edges, so the creases alone are 15.
s: Names the error: the increases double, so the next is 16
Gives 33 after 5 folds
States the rule 2^n + 1
Gets 65 after 6 folds
Gets 15 creases after 4 folds

questions.q: Aarav looks at two lines u and v in a picture. They look as if they will meet far away, so he says they are not parallel. Bhavna cuts them with a straight line and finds the corresponding angles are 70 degrees and 70 degrees. Compare the two ways of deciding: say which can be trusted and why, what Bhavna should conclude, what angle she would expect for a pair of alternate angles between the lines, and what pair of readings such as 70 and 74 degrees would have meant.
questions.a: Aarav's way, judging by eye, can be misled, since the chapter shows that it is difficult to be sure just by looking. Bhavna's way, with a transversal, can be trusted. Her corresponding angles are equal, so u and v are parallel. Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal, so she would expect 70 degrees. Corresponding angles of 70 and 74 would be unequal, so the lines would not be parallel.
s: Says the eye judgement can mislead
Says the transversal method is reliable
Concludes parallel because 70 = 70
Expects an alternate angle of 70 degrees
Says 70 and 74 would mean not parallel

questions.q:
In art class in Kolkata, Ananya folds a square sheet horizontally in half, then in half again, and so on, opening it each time to count the parallel lines, the two edges included. The first fold takes 1 minute, and each later fold takes twice as long as the one before (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 minutes). She needs at least 30 parallel lines on one sheet and has 35 minutes. A line drawn with a ruler and a set square takes 1 minute and is parallel to the fold lines.
(a) How many parallel lines does she have after 4 folds, and how long did that take? (b) How many lines after 5 folds, and how long in all? (c) After 4 folds, how many extra lines must she draw with the ruler to reach 30, and how long would the whole plan take? (d) Both plans fit in 35 minutes. Which should she choose and why?
questions.a: (a) 2^4 + 1 = 17 lines; time 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 minutes. (b) 2^5 + 1 = 33 lines; time 15 + 16 = 31 minutes. (c) 30 - 17 = 13 extra lines; the plan takes 15 + 13 = 28 minutes. (d) The plan of 4 folds plus 13 ruled lines, because it finishes in 28 minutes, 3 minutes sooner than 5 folds (31 minutes); both give at least 30 parallel lines.
s: Part (a): 17 lines and 15 minutes
Part (b): 33 lines and 31 minutes
Part (c): 13 extra lines and 28 minutes
Part (d): picks the 28 minute plan since it is 3 minutes sooner

questions.q:
A designer is making a stone lattice for a haveli in Jaipur. Three long lines p, q and r are cut across it, and a straight edge t crosses all three. In the same position, t makes 58 degrees with p, 58 degrees with q and 61 degrees with r. To the eye, p and r look parallel while q looks slanted. For the design all three must be parallel. Option 1: re-cut r so that its angle with t becomes 58 degrees, at a cost of ₹800. Option 2: re-cut p and q so that each makes 61 degrees with t, at ₹500 per line.
(a) Which two lines are parallel, and why? (b) Is r parallel to p? Why? (c) By how many degrees does r have to turn if only r is re-cut? (d) Which option is cheaper, and what do you recommend?
questions.a: (a) p and q, because their corresponding angles with t are equal (58 and 58). (b) No, since 58 is not equal to 61. The looks are misleading. (c) 3 degrees. (d) Re-cutting only r costs ₹800; re-cutting p and q costs 2 x 500 = ₹1,000. Re-cutting only r is cheaper, so recommend that.
s: Part (a): names p and q with the equal corresponding angles reason
Part (b): says not parallel since 58 is not 61
Part (c): says 3 degrees
Part (d): compares 800 with 1,000 and recommends re-cutting only r
